issues.legal_issue: A father's self-acquired property inherited by his sons when no grandsons had been born is held by the sons as co-heirs, not as joint Hindu family property.
material_facts: The family elder owned the properties as his self-acquired property.
When the elder died, he left three sons and no grandsons had been born to them.
The sons obtained the properties by inheritance, and descendants of two branches later sought partition.
issues.conclusion: The inherited properties were not joint Hindu family properties; they were held as property of co-heirs, capable of partition on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the Madras Full Bench decision in Viravan Chettiar v. Srinivasachariar, the Court held that a son has no enforceable birthright in his father's self-acquired property and has only a spes successionis; without an enforceable right to partition, there is no coparcenary in that property. The Court relied on the reasoning in Balwant Singh v. Rani Kishore, Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Deoraj Kuari, and Raja Chelikant Venkayamma v. Raja Chelikani Venkataramanayamma. It noted that section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 provides that heirs succeeding together take per capita and as tenants-in-common, not joint tenants. The Court followed the settled Madras view without resolving the wider conflict among High Courts.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and father_owned_self_acquired_property and no_grandsons_at_inheritance and sons_succeeded_by_inheritance

predicates.partition_proceeding: The claimants sought division of property held among family members.
predicates.father_owned_self_acquired_property: The father had acquired the property himself.
predicates.no_grandsons_at_inheritance: No sons of the father's sons had been born when the father died.
predicates.sons_succeeded_by_inheritance: The father's sons obtained the property upon his death by inheritance.

issues.definition: When a partition claim concerns self-acquired property inherited by sons while no grandsons had been born, the sons hold it as co-heirs rather than as a joint family.

issues.legal_issue: Property purchased from income derived from property held by co-owners is accountable as their shared property, not as joint Hindu family property.
material_facts: The parties held the inherited properties as co-owners.
Some disputed properties were said to have been purchased from income derived from the inherited properties.
The defendants failed to prove their plea of adverse possession, and the Court left that factual finding undisturbed.
The accounting for the accreted property remained to be determined before the final decree.
issues.conclusion: If the accreted property was purchased from income derived from the property held in common, it had to be accounted for as shared property, not as joint Hindu family property; the accounting was to be determined before the final decree.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that property purchased from income derived from property held by co-owners is accountable as their shared property and does not thereby acquire the character of joint Hindu family property. It also observed that a plea of adverse possession inherently asserts that another person owns the property; the defendants' failure to prove that plea left the factual finding undisturbed. No earlier case was cited for this clarification.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and coowners_held_source_property and accretion_bought_with_source_income and adverse_possession_claim_failed

predicates.partition_proceeding: The claimants sought division of property held among family members.
predicates.coowners_held_source_property: The parties held the property that generated the income as co-owners.
predicates.accretion_bought_with_source_income: The disputed additional property was purchased using income derived from the co-owned property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_failed: The party asserting adverse possession did not prove that claim.

issues.definition: In a partition proceeding, an acquisition made with income from property held by co-owners is accounted for as shared property, rather than joint family property, when the stated facts apply.
